doc.title: Arthur Baron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Baron's upbringing, Black Lives Matter and urging listeners to speak out
summary: Baron recalls a white upper-middle-class background with little contact with Black people, praises Brian Lehrer, affirms Black Lives Matter and encourages others to speak up.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Privilege, that’s the perfect word. And I don’t like that. So we called up all these people and had various responses but all extremely positive. And there was also something, when you bring a conversation up to the next level, when you say what you have to say, there’s a pause. Because our black friends hadn’t heard anything like this from us. And then they came in and spoke and boy I’ll tell you my wife and I were nervous during that pause. Did we do something wrong? Are we too liberal? Are we too something? And it never was the case. And I also have to give credit to my wife Ingvild. Because I said look, she said, “I’m shy, you do the talking.” I said, “This is your idea and I don’t want it to sound like it was my idea.” I asked her about it today. I’m going to put it in FaceBook and make it very clear it’s her idea. Because I’ve been thinking about these issues for years and not knowing what to do about it. What do you do? It’s like, you know, I mean Benny Johnson the drummer, I don’t know if you ever knew of him, a wonderful black drummer friend of mine. And he drove me to a lot of gigs with The Duke’s Men. We got really, really tight. And we covered some ground together and that was good because we spent a lot of time together. But I come from a background of middle white class. Upper middle white class, or middle to upper, where the only blacks I saw were criminals going to prison on television news, and garbage men. And man, you know those tapes, they exist. And like I finally in high school had a couple of black students and a few of them and I got to be friends. You know it’s like they’re people. I heard, you know a great show to listen to you, you won’t get it in the air but online you can get on WNYC public radio down in New York, 10 to 12 every weekday, Brian Lehrer, he has an amazing call-in

show and it’s just continuing. And they bring up all these issues. You know it’s just, I mean I think, I mean it took a pandemic and then to have a brutal killing of a man, a man first, then put a black man. Black Lives Matter. And one thing I’ve got to say, I understand. This is not the time to be spouting out white lives matter too. We got the privilege. We don’t need to hear that. What we need to hear is what I just said, Black Lives Matter. And I believe this happened and it was more intense, more stirring the pot because it’s during the pandemic. And that’s good. I mean it’s not good he got killed. Nothing good about it. But if we can make something good come out of it then we’re being blessed.
Thanks for sharing that. Very important.

Yeah and I hope if you’re listening people, take a chance. Even if it’s like you go into a store and a black man or a Hispanic man is running it, or woman, or friends, anything, just speak the truth. Hopefully it is your truth that you want to let them know you stand by them.
